shots.text: Four soldiers picked up a Sherman tank and carried it across a field.
Two French cyclists stop dead. One soldier just shrugs. "Americans are very strong."
Wait, what? Well, you see, that tank weighs ninety-three pounds. It's made of rubber.
In nineteen forty-four, America sends about eleven hundred men to France with one job. Look like thirty thousand.
And they aren't fighters. They're painters, designers and actors.
Every night, they blow up rubber tanks and paint fake markings on trucks.
Huge speakers play tanks rolling, heard fifteen miles away.
Fake radio operators even copy the real operators' Morse code style.
But one close look, and the whole trick is over.
You see, a spy plane sees shapes, not weight. Like a cardboard cutout in a shop window, it looks real from across the street.
Then one night in March nineteen forty-five, they build a fake army by the Rhine. German troops move to face it. The real army crosses miles away.
And the eleven hundred men? They go home, and can't tell a soul for fifty years.
